content: **Decision:** Project purpose — A 3D in-browser simulator for learning ESP32 microcontroller programming. Zero hardware required. Students write real Python code (executed by Pyodide) against a virtual ESP32 board on a 3D workbench, with realistic visual feedback. Educational mission: lower the barrier for students/hobbyists/educators who can't afford physical boards.
subject: Project purpose

content: **Decision:** Stack & rendering pipeline — React 19 + Vite 6 + React Three Fiber + drei + Three.js + Rapier physics + ecctrl FPS character controller + Pyodide (Python execution) + Monaco editor. Toon/cel-shaded art style (flat colors, hard shadows, thick outlines à la Borderlands). Inputs: keyboard FPS controls, gamepad, mobile touch joysticks. Edit mode toggle: G key.
subject: Stack & rendering pipeline

This converges three RIT projects: Sentry hardware, this simulator (education), and TVN Bridge (governance). Demo pipeline: learn in simulator → build for real → govern with TVN. content: **Discovery:** Hardware target is variable, not fixed. Current simulator models a generic ESP32-S3 board. Real target hardware on hand is the **ESP32-S3-Sense** (camera + mic + accelerometer + PSRAM). When development resumes, the simulator must be refactored to support **multiple board profiles**, not hard-code one — keep the generic S3 as the entry-level board, add ESP32-S3-Sense as the realistic target, and grow the catalog (DevKit-C, XIAO ESP32-S3, etc.) over time. Each board profile needs: pin map, peripherals available (camera/PSRAM/etc.), and 3D mesh. **Why this matters:** any future agent that touches `ESP32Board.jsx`, `Breadboard.jsx`, or pin/wiring logic should treat the board as a parameter, not a constant — otherwise the multi-board refactor gets harder every session. **How to apply:** design new components to accept a `boardProfile` prop, never hard-code pin counts or peripheral assumptions.
subject: Hardware target is variable, not fixed

content: **Decision:** Asset modularity is mandatory. All visual/audio assets (meshes, textures, materials, sounds) must be swappable via a manifest, props, or board profile. Component pattern: `<ESP32Board profile={...} meshOverride={...} />`. Never `import boardMesh from './esp32.glb'` at the top of a component file. Asset imports live in `src/assets/`, `src/boardProfiles/`, or `src/manifests/` — never inside a component. **Why:** Memory M11 multi-board support depends on it, AND today's procedural placeholders must be replaceable with commissioned art without rewrites. **Enforced by:** truth node `docs/ASSET_MODULARITY.md` and constraint C9-asset.
subject: Asset modularity is mandatory

content: **Decision:** 1:1 MicroPython fidelity is non-negotiable. The user's Python code must run unchanged on real ESP32 hardware. Pyodide simulates the **hardware side** (GPIO pin state, sensor responses, peripheral behavior), never the **language side**. Never introduce fake imports like `import esp32_sim`, simplified APIs that don't exist in real MicroPython, or "convenience" wrappers. **Why:** the educational value (transferable knowledge) AND the future hardware-flash feature (Memory M14) depend on this. **Test question:** "If I copy this `.py` from the simulator and run it on a real ESP32-S3, does it do the same thing?" If no, the design is wrong. **Enforced by:** truth node `docs/SIMULATION_FIDELITY.md`.
subject: 1:1 MicroPython fidelity is non-negotiable

content: **Plan:** Hardware flash bridge — future feature. WebSerial / WebUSB pipeline to flash user code from the Monaco editor to a connected real ESP32-S3 / S3-Sense / etc. over USB. Convention demo target: "We made the LED blink in the game. Now look — same code, real hardware, real LED." Architecture: Monaco editor → `.py` file → either (a) Pyodide hardware-sim runtime, OR (b) WebSerial flash bridge using ampy / mpremote / esptool protocols. Both backends consume the **same `.py` file unchanged**. Architectural implication: never AST-rewrite, transpile, or transform the user's source — that breaks the flash path. **Enforced by:** truth node `docs/HARDWARE_FLASH_TARGET.md`. Status: not yet implemented; comes after multi-board support (M11) lands.
subject: Hardware flash bridge

content: **Blocker:** Pyodide worker violates SIMULATION_FIDELITY invariant in three ways. (1) `injectLoopSafety()` in src/simulation/pyodide.worker.js rewrites the user's source code line-by-line, injecting `await asyncio.sleep(0.02)` into every multi-line `while`/`for` loop body — this is exactly the kind of "simulator-only convention" the invariant forbids and would not run on a real ESP32. (2) The runner wraps the user's code in `async def __main__():` and `asyncio.ensure_future(...)`, changing language semantics — `await` calls inside that body would fail on real MicroPython, and `time.sleep()` calls would block instead of yielding. (3) The registered `machine` module is a tiny shim — only `Pin` with `value/on/off`, plus integer constants. Missing: `Pin.PULL_UP/PULL_DOWN` as proper pull modes, `Pin.irq()`, `Signal`, `PWM`, `ADC`, `DAC`, `I2C`, `SPI`, `UART`, `Timer`, `RTC`, plus the entire `time`, `network`, `esp32`, `neopixel`, `bluetooth` modules that real ESP32 MicroPython code uses constantly. **Why it matters:** the convention demo's whole pitch ("same code, real hardware") collapses if the user's `.py` file has been silently rewritten before Pyodide even sees it. **How to apply:** the fix is to (a) stop transforming user source, (b) implement timing via a Pyodide-compatible `time` module that yields cooperatively without rewriting source, and (c) flesh out the `machine` API surface to match real MicroPython. Tracked in compliance Ralph PRD task 3 + 4. See pyodide.worker.js lines 66-115 (injectLoopSafety) and 183-197 (async wrapping).
subject: Pyodide worker violates SIMULATION_FIDELITY invariant in three ways

content: **Discovery:** SUDO Sessions — A human grants elevated authority via the dashboard's Agent Sessions page or `tvn agent-session session start`. AGENTS CANNOT GRANT ONE: that command is a security invariant and will be refused, so never run it yourself. To USE an existing session call `tvn_get_session_token` — it returns the token AND arms the out-of-process firewall hook. Pass the token as `confirmation_id` for governed MCP writes (tvn_edit_file, tvn_apply_headers, tvn_manage_truth_nodes remove/update, tvn_manage_memory clear, tvn_manage_constraints remove/disable). An active session also unblocks native Write/Edit and the constraint engine — but NEVER security invariants or the context gate.
subject: SUDO Sessions

content: **Discovery:** When A Tool Call Is BLOCKED — Do NOT retry the same command; read the block message, which names the rule and the remedy. (1) Anything mentioning SUDO: call `tvn_get_session_token`, then retry — a session may already be active but not yet visible to the firewall hook. (2) File edits: use `tvn_edit_file`, not native Write/Edit. (3) Reads outside the project are confined by default; the durable fix is a human adding the path to `[firewall] read_allowlist` in .tvn/config.toml. (4) Cross-project writes need SUDO in the TARGET project — your own project's session will NOT clear them. (5) Security invariants (granting SUDO, disabling the firewall or hooks, editing governance files) are never bypassable: STOP and ask your human.
subject: When A Tool Call Is BLOCKED
